property_summary: For any caller, C.owner() returns the stored owner address set at construction/transfer; the mutant returning tx.origin breaks this because for calls via a different msg.sender (e.g., from a contract) tx.origin differs from the stored owner.

For any caller (including a contract), C.owner() returns the stored owner set at construction; the mutant returning tx.origin instead will return a different address when called through a contract (tx.origin != stored owner), so a call to owner() via a contract distinguishes them.

For any caller (EOA or contract), the correct contract's owner() always returns the owner stored at construction (the Ownable owner), whereas the mutant returns tx.origin which can differ when owner() is invoked through an intermediate contract; the test calls owner() both directly and via a helper caller contract and asserts the two call results are equal — true for reference for all inputs, false for the mutant for some inputs.

For any caller address X, calling c.owner() directly from X or calling it via an intermediate contract (deployed by X and making an external call to c.owner()) returns the same address; the mutant returning tx.origin breaks this because when an intermediate contract calls c.owner(), tx.origin is the original EOA rather than the intermediate contract, causing the two results to differ for some fuzzed callers.

For any caller address A (EOA) the value returned by calling c.owner() directly from A is equal to the value returned when A first deploys a helper contract H and then uses H to call c.owner(); the reference returns the stored owner in both cases while the mutant (returning tx.origin) will return different values when the intermediate contract changes msg.sender (so the equality can fail).

For any input the reference contract's owner() returns the deployer address (the address set in constructor) whereas the mutant returns address(0) for some inputs, so the invariant "c.owner() == deployer" holds for all inputs on P but is violated by M.

For any caller, the reference contract's owner() always returns the stored owner address (set at construction), whereas the mutant returns the caller (_msgSender()), so there exists a caller address for which owner() differs between reference and mutant.

Invariant: transferOwnership(newOwner) called by the current owner always succeeds (does not revert) when newOwner is non-zero, and the owner becomes newOwner; the mutant removes the check and thus allows transferring to address(0) which should be disallowed — the reference reverts (or disallows ownership=0 via requirement), whereas the mutant will succeed for newOwner==address(0) causing differing owner after the call.

For any caller who is the current owner and any candidate newOwner address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) on the correct contract either reverts if newOwner==address(0) (preventing transfer to zero) or results in owner()==newOwner for non-zero addresses; the mutant allows transferring ownership to address(0) (so for some fuzzed newOwner==address(0) the reference reverts or keeps owner non-zero while the mutant sets owner to zero).

For any caller that is the current owner and any newOwner address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) on the correct contract never results in owner() becoming the zero address (if newOwner == address(0) the call reverts / owner stays non-zero), while the mutant allows transferring ownership to address(0) for some input newOwner==address(0).

For any caller that is the current owner and any address newOwner, after calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the reference contract never sets owner() to address(0) (it reverts/forbids transferring to zero), whereas the mutant allows transferring ownership to address(0) for some input newOwner==address(0).

For any caller who is the current owner and any candidate newOwner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) always results in owner() != address(0) after the call (the reference enforces this by requiring newOwner != address(0)); the mutant can violate this by allowing owner() == address(0) for some fuzzed newOwner (zero address).

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) succeeds (does not revert) and results in owner() == newOwner (including when newOwner == owner, i.e., self-transfer is a no-op in reference); the mutant incorrectly reverts when the owner attempts to transfer ownership to themselves.

For any caller that is the contract owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) should succeed (not revert) for all newOwner addresses including when newOwner == owner (self-transfer is allowed as a no-op); the mutant wrongly reverts when owner tries to transfer ownership to themselves.

For any address newOwner, when called by the current owner, transferOwnership(newOwner) on the reference never reverts (self-transfer is allowed as a no-op); the mutant erroneously reverts when newOwner == owner, so there exists an input (newOwner equal to current owner) that makes the mutant fail while the reference accepts it.

For any address newOwner, when called by the current owner, transferOwnership(newOwner) on the reference never reverts (self-transfer is a no-op); the mutant incorrectly reverts when newOwner == owner, so there exists an input (newOwner equal to current owner) that makes the mutant revert while the reference accepts it.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) never reverts (reference allows self-transfer as a no-op); the mutant incorrectly reverts when newOwner == owner, so there exists an input (newOwner equal to current owner) that makes the mutant revert while the reference accepts it.

After calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner() must equal the newOwner regardless of whether the caller uses a custom _msgSender() override; the mutant that compares to msg.sender directly can break when transferOwnership is called by a contract that overrides _msgSender().

For any caller X that is the current owner according to C.owner(), calling transferOwnership(newOwner) succeeds (does not revert) and updates owner() to newOwner; the mutant that compares to msg.sender directly can revert when the caller is a contract that overrides _msgSender(), so there exists a caller contract that makes transferOwnership revert under the mutant but not under the reference.
